current.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent walk-off. From the true summit, most parties make three single-rope (30 m) rappels down the tower to a small, exposed high notch, then one longer double-rope (60 m) rappel from that notch down into the gully/glacier below — roughly four rappels in typical late-summer, snow-free conditions. Anchors along this line are almost entirely improvised rather than bolted: slung boulders, horns and pedestals wrapped with tat/cord, and the occasional jammed knot in a crack; a couple of the stations have accumulated enough old cord to look semi-permanent, but none should be trusted blindly and back-up/extend as needed. Bring a single 60 m rope (or two ropes if you want to do the notch-to-glacier drop as one clean pull rather than downclimbing part of it). In seasons or conditions where a snow finger lingers in the descent gully, parties have needed far more — up to 9-10 shorter single-rope rappels interspersed with downclimbing to get through the same 400-ft gully system, because a lingering snow patch prevents a clean full-length pull; budget extra time and a plan B if you find snow still choking the gully. Known hazards on this descent: persistently loose, choss-prone rock (the Southeast Spire's rock quality is poor, and at least one incident involved a slab breaking loose during rope retrieval at the notch and striking a climber), ropes getting stuck when pulled through the loose gully, high exposure along the east ledges near the Ridge of Gendarmes, and fatigue/darkness on the lower-angle terrain given how long this climb runs. After reaching the glacier below the Col of the Wild, reverse the approach traverse back to your high camp (Redoubt Col/Ouzel Lake), then descend the Depot Creek climbers path past the falls — using the fixed handline again on the steep slab section — back to the trailhead.

current.rappels: Rappel the East Face on its own line, about a dozen or more rappels on doubled ropes over roughly 2,400 ft, every anchor built from slung horns, chockstones and gear: there are no bolts anywhere on the route. No station list is published.
current.rappel_count_note: The only documented descent is the first ascent’s, which rappelled the face top to bottom on natural anchors, roughly a dozen-plus rappels; no station list or count has been published since, so none is shown. On that descent the first rappel hung up and had to be freed by climbing back to the top, and the anchors were angled toward the northeast ridge to find sounder rock than the ascent line.
current.descent_text: The East Face is rappelled top to bottom on its own line — there is no walk-off, and no fixed/bolted rappel stations exist anywhere on the route; every anchor is natural (slung horns, chockstones/gear anchors) built on the spot, so a party needs full natural-anchor-building skill and a rack sufficient to leave gear behind. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) rappelled the entire 2,400-2,500 ft face using two ropes tied together to maximize each rappel's reach, angling the line closer to the northeast ridge than their ascent line, especially on the lower half, to find sounder anchor rock and avoid the loosest terrain in the direct fall line. Their first rappel hung up and forced a strenuous full return to the top to free it before they could continue; from there, roughly a dozen more rappels (about 13 total) got them to the ground, finishing around 3:30 a.m. after an 18-hour continuous push from the base. At the bottom they waded back across the creek chest-deep rather than re-entering the alder/devil's club to reach their tent. Later parties should plan on a similar count (very roughly a dozen-plus rappels with a doubled/joined-rope setup) but treat that as an estimate scaled from a single documented descent, not a fixed number — anchor placement is judgment-call and can shift the rappel line and count. Expect loose, sometimes rotten rock the entire way (a defining hazard of the route), real risk of stuck ropes given the wandering natural-anchor line, and likely a night finish if the climb runs long, so headlamps and a plan for rope work in the dark should be assumed.

current.descent_text: The descent does not reverse the ridge. Both of the route's rappels — about 25 m into the gap at the Pitch 7 gendarme and about 30 m off the final hoodoo tower — are made on the way up, below the last ~600 ft of scrambling to the top, so a single 60 m rope covers them. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. From the summit, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, relaxed steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the usual endless scree and loose talus that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.
